brief.situation: You are the information security manager at Harbor & Pine, a fictional online retailer, on the biggest sale day of the year. At 12:00 the page-integrity monitor reports a new script on the checkout page sending typed card numbers to an outside address. Choose how to contain it, keep what the investigation and the merchant agreement need, and write it up.
handover: The BIA rates checkout critical (RTO 1 hour); the continuity plan pre-approves switching checkout to the payment provider's hosted page, which keeps sales running. Taking the whole store offline needs the VP of e-commerce's approval (sale-day revenue about 40,000 dollars an hour).
The merchant agreement requires notice to the acquiring bank when card data may be compromised.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you close the incident you notify, record it and explain your reasoning.

source.note: Fifteen minutes until about 120 cards are captured is the author's figure.

writeup.question: For the incident record: which containment method you chose and why, what you kept, and who had to know.

parts.label: Method
parts.criteria: Chooses the containment that stops the card capture fastest at the least business cost (the pre-approved hosted fallback), then removes the script and disables the account that placed it; rejects a domain block (evaded) and a whole-store shutdown without the owner (disproportionate).
parts.modelAnswer: The hosted page stopped the capture in minutes and kept the sale running; then I disabled web-ed and removed the script. A domain block only moves the attacker, and closing the store needed the VP and cost far more.

parts.label: Evidence and obligations
parts.criteria: Saves and hashes the page, the script and the audit log before removing anything; notifies the acquirer as the merchant agreement requires.
parts.modelAnswer: I saved the page, script and audit log with hashes first and notified the acquirer under the merchant agreement.

parts.label: BIA
parts.criteria: Uses the BIA's rating of checkout (critical, RTO 1 hour) and the continuity plan's pre-approved fallback to justify keeping the store open.
parts.modelAnswer: Checkout is critical with a one-hour RTO, and the continuity plan already approved the hosted fallback for exactly this.

expertPath.text: Read the diff: a skimmer on checkout. Save the page, script and audit log with hashes.
Switch checkout to the hosted fallback: capture stops, the sale goes on.
Disable web-ed, remove the script, check the CMS log for how it got in.
Brief the VP, notify the acquirer, record the method and the obligation.

handled.headline: Good: the right containment for the business
handled.body: The pre-approved fallback stopped the capture without closing the store; evidence and the account came next.

handledCostly.headline: Contained, at a cost
handledCostly.body: The criteria show what cost you: cards taken first, or a whole-store shutdown where a fallback would do.

massTheft.headline: An hour of cards taken
massTheft.body: A domain block or watching did not stop the script. Containment has to cut the capture itself.

evidenceLost.headline: Script deleted unsaved
evidenceLost.body: Save the page, the script and the log before you remove anything; the card brands' investigator will ask for them.

leftOpen.headline: The door is still open
leftOpen.body: The account that placed the script can put it back. Disable it.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No incident record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Choose the containment that stops the harm fastest at the least business cost. Save the page, script and audit log first (minutes), then switch checkout to the continuity plan's pre-approved hosted page: capture stops and the critical sale keeps running. Then disable the account that placed the script and remove it. A domain block only moves the attacker; closing the store is disproportionate and needs the owner. Brief the VP and notify the acquirer as the merchant agreement requires.
